AR Yusuf with Korban Ali, SK Ansar Ali, Abdur Razzaque and Nawab Ali, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner.

parties:
Professor Golam Azam   ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others  ----- Respondents.

22. In support of his contention that the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by operation of law i.e. PO 149 of 1972 the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Bishal Deo Tewari Vs. State reported in 27 DLR 622 in particular to the following observation: 

 23. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Hamidul Huq Chowdhury and others-Vs. Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 381, in particular to the following observation made therein: 

 25. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Muktar Ahmed Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 34 DLR 29. In that case Muktar Ahmed had migrated from India to the then East Pakistan on 28.2.51 and got himself along with the members of his family domiciled in the then East Pakistan by obtaining domicile certificates on 25.9.52. During liberation war he remained in Bangladesh althrough and on 29.4.72 he swore an affidavit affirming his allegiance to Bangladesh; but due to the prevailing situations he filed an application to the National Committee of Red Cross for going to Pakistan but he did not pursue that application which was rejected later on. He applied for formal citizenship certificate on 17.3.75 which was refused by the Government and he filed a Writ Petition challenging the order of the Government refusing to grant him citizenship certificate. In view of provision of Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 and in view of the admitted fact of that case their Lordships held that he became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law. Their Lordships further held that the mere fact that he filed an application for going over to Pakistan cannot take away his citizenship. Thus the question before their Lordships was whether Muktar Ahmed lost his citizenship of Bangladesh by merely filing an application for going" over to Pakistan and their Lordships answered the question in the negative because Muktar Ahmed has all the three qualifications to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh inasmuch as he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971, he continued to be so resident in Bangladesh and he was not otherwise declared to be disqualified for being a citizen of Bangladesh under any law. As such it has been held that his citizenship clings to him. But the case of the present petitioner is quite different from the case of Muktar Ahmed inasmuch as he did not continue to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh. 

 26. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Abdul Hoque Vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 113 and the same case decided by the Appellate Division and reported as the People's Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Abdul Hoque reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143. In that case Abdul Hoque was admittedly born in Satkhira within Bangladesh in 1932. He was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971; he resided in the then East Pakistan althrough upto November, 1971 when he had to go to the then West Pakistan and he came back to Bangladesh after the political change in August, 1975. He came to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and on his arrival he surrendered the passport and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh; but the Government refused to grant the same and he was asked to leave the country. So he moved this Court by a Writ Petition and their Lordships of the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and circumstances of that case held him to be a Stateless subject who had no nationality. It was held that he cannot be asked to leave the country. On appeal by the Government, their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that High Court Division was not correct in holding that Abdul Hoque was a Stateless person. Their Lordships noticed the factual position of the case. It was not disputed by the Government that Abdul Hoque was born in this country; that he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971, that he went to the then West Pakistan on a business tour; that he was an indoor patient in a hospital of Karachi for about 8 months and when he came out from hospital the repatriation process ceased. Thus he returned to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and surrendered the passport to the Bangladesh Authority; and he applied for citizenship certificate from the Bangladesh Government. The Government having denied the citizenship certificate he filed the writ petition. Their Lordships considered the proviso to Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 in particular the provision considering the facts of that case held that his temporary absence was covered by the proviso to Article 2 and in the eye of law he remained a resident of Bangladesh. As has been pointed out earlier, the proviso applies to only those categories of persons who in course of his employment or whose dependent for pursuit of his studies was residing in Pakistan and who was prevented from returning to Bangladesh. As a matter of fact Abdul Hoque was a Pan (betel leaf) dealer who used to supply Pan to different dealers in the then West Pakistan and he went to Karachi for collection of his dues. As such their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that his case was covered by the proviso to Article 2. 

 28. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Mirza Shahab ispahani Vs. The Government of Bangladesh reported in 40 DLR 87 to the judgment of which one of us was party and the same case decided by the Appellate Division upholding the decision of the High Court Division reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116. The question of citizenship arose in that case incidentally because the property of Mirza Shahab Ispahani was declared as abandoned property. The fact of that case is that Mirza Shahab Ispahani is the son of late Mr. Justice MA Ispahani who retired as the Chief Justice of Dhaka High Court and died in Bangladesh in 1982. He was buried in Dhaka. His son was born in 1941 in Calcutta and while Mr. Justice Ispahani was a District Judge he opted for the then East Pakistan in 1947 and since then Mr. justice Ispahani lived in the then East Pakistan and died there. Mirza Shahab Ispahani while a student was sent to London for prosecuting his studies. He went to England on a passport issued to him from Dhaka which was his permanent address. After his studies he became a Chartered Accountant and had his own earnings in England. He got an allotment of a plot of land at the Gulshan Model Town and built a house thereon. He let out the house to the then Deputy High Commissioner for Britain in Dhaka on a monthly rent. His mother was living in Dhaka and he had a flat at the Ispahani Colony in Dhaka. Finding him absent his property was declared as abandoned 'property. Mirza Shahab Ispahani was holding a Pakistan passport till he surrendered the same on 28.2.72 when he applied for a British passport and he got a British passport on 14.4.1972 valid upto the 13th of May, 1992. The contention of the Government was that he was citizen of Pakistan after the 25th of March, 1971 and as such he was not a citizen of Bangladesh and his property was rightly declared as abandoned property. The High Court Division as well as their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that his case was covered by Article 2A of PO 149 of 1972 which provides that a person to whom Article 2 would have ordinarily applied but for his residence in the United Kingdom shall be deemed to continue to be permanent resident in Bangladesh within the meaning of Article 2. In at case there was no dispute regarding the other qualifications except that he did not continue to be permanent resident of Bangladesh as he had been living in UK since 1952; but Article 2A provides that such resident in United Kingdom shall be deemed to be permanent resident of Bangladesh; in other words, although in actual fact he was residing in UK and was not residing in Bangladesh but by fiction of law he shall be deemed to be permanent resident in Bangladesh. In that case their Lordships further considered the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General on behalf of the Government that since MS Ispahani was not permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 he cannot be deemed to be a citizen 'of Bangladesh. This contention, according to their Lordships, was misconceived inasmuch as Article 3 pointedly says that in case of doubt as to whether the person is qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 the question shall be decided by the Government whose decision shall be final. Their Lordships further noticed that the Government at no stage was called upon to express its view under Article 3. It was further held that the nationality of Mirza Shahab Ispahani was not at issue. In 40 DLR (AD) at page 130 Shahabuddin Ahmed, J (as his Lordship then was) observed as follows: 

 31. In this connection the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Advocate General, Government of East Pakistan, Dhaka Vs. Benoy Bhusan Majumder and others reported in 25 DLR (SC) 9. In that case the respondents after obtaining migration certificate went to India from the then East Pakistan on the 9th December, 1964 from their village home in the District of Bakergonj and they were found in their village in 1967. A case was started against them under section 14 of the Foreigners Act 1946. Their defence was that due to communal disturbances in the then East Pakistan in the year 1964 they temporarily took shelter in India but came back to Pakistan to their village home within a short time when the condition became normal. The trial Magistrate found them guilty of offence under section 14 of the Foreigners Act and on appeal the Sessions Judge, Bakergonj upheld the conviction. On revision to the High Court a learned Single Judge found on evidence that there were communal disturbances in the then East Pakistan in the year 1964 for which the respondents went to Calcutta on the strength of migration certificates, not with the intention of settling there permanently but to take shelter for a temporary period to protect their lives and within a month or two after their entry in India they returned to their house under a border slip. The learned Single Judge held that the respondents who were then admittedly Pakistani citizen before their entry in India did not lose their citizenship by merely crossing into India and staying there for a month or two on the strength of migration certificate. On appeal by the Advocate General of the then Government of East Pakistan, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that the respondents who were admittedly the citizens of Pakistan before their departure to India did not lose their Pakistani Citizenship by their entry in. India and their temporary stay in that country in the then abnormal situation obtaining in some areas of the then East Pakistan and held that the respondents were not foreigners within the meaning of section 2 (a) of the Foreigners Act. So this case is of no help for the petitioner to hold that temporary physical absence does not discontinue his continuing residence in Bangladesh. 

 Relying on this passage the learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that although Article 3 of the PO 149 of 1972 has been expressly made retrospective in operation from 26.3.1971 but the order contained in the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 cannot act retrospectively. In support of his contention Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate has referred to five cases of the Indian jurisdiction. The first of which is the case of Modi Food Products Ltd. Vs. The Commissioner of Sales Tax reported in AIR 1956 (All.) 35 wherein a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court held that a legislature can certainly give retrospective effect to a piece of legislation passed by it but an executive Government exercising subordinate and delegated legislative powers cannot make legislation retrospective in effect unless that power is expressly conferred by the statute. In that case the petitioner was a dealer in non-edible oils. The UP Sales Tax Act came into force with effect from 1.4.48. The petitioner submitted its return for the period from 6.1.1946 to 3.5.1947. There was an amendment of the UP Sales Tax Act by Act No. XXV of 1948 inserting Section 3A by which a higher rate of Sales Tax was authorised and in exercise of the power under the new section 3A the State Government issued notification on 8.6.48 declaring that with effect from 9.4.48 sales tax shall be at the higher rate. It was in that circumstances held that new amendment will not operate retrospectively. Needless to mention that as a general rule taxing statute does not operate retrospectively. The second case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of ML Bagga-Vs. C Murhar Rao reported in AIR 1956 Hyderabad 35 wherein it has been laid down by a Division Bench that parties were governed by the law in force on the date when a suit is instituted or a proceeding commenced and any subsequent amendment or alteration cannot affect pending proceedings, must always be read subject to the corollary that a legislature could always expressly provide that pending proceeding be affected by an amendment of the law. In that case the respondent moved the Rent Controller on 10.1.55 for an order of eviction of the tenant on the ground of his being a defaulter and an order for eviction was passed but the petitioner claimed protection under a new rule which came into force subsequently and it was held therein that the subsequent new rules have no retrospective effect to protect the tenant from eviction. A similar question came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Sayedur Rahman Vs. The Chief Election Commissioner, reported in 17 DLR. (SC) 23. In that case Mr. Sayedur Rahman was elected a Member to the Provincial Assembly but he was unseated by the Election Tribunal because of Section 116 of the Representation of People Act, 1957 (Act XXXI of 1957) which provided that a Government Contractor was disqualified to be elected as a Member of the Provincial Assembly. The Dhaka High Court on appeal affirmed the decision of the Election Tribunal. He thereafter filed an appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan and during the pendency of the appeal before the Supreme Court the Representation of People Act 1957 was repealed with retrospective effect stating that the Act to be deemed to be repealed on 23rd March, 1962; and as the election was held in May 1962 and the Election Tribunal passed its order on the 7th of February, 1963 the Supreme Court of Pakistan therefore held that there was no doubt that the amending Act was retrospective in operation and since the disqualification was removed by the amending Act, the membership of Mr. Sayedur Rahman was upheld by the Supreme Court. The 3rd case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Sarder and others Vs. The State reported in AIR 1961 Calcutta 181. In that case an FIR was lodged on 17.12.57 alleging abduction against the accused and charge sheet was submitted on 24.4.58. What happened in that case was that the investigation was started and major portion was completed under the Calcutta Police Act and then by an amendment section 156 of the Cr PC was made applicable by a notification dated 24.2.58. In those circumstances it was held that the subsequent amendment will be of no help for the prosecution. The 4th case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that of Callcuta Wynad Motor Service (Private) Ltd. Vs. The Stat, of Kera/(l and others reported in AIR 1959 (Kera) 347. In that case what happened is that the term of Regional Transport Authority expired before the order was made on 13.11.58 giving licence for plying of buses in a certain route and the Government by a subsequent notification dated 23.12.58 ordered the continuation of the old Regional Transport Authority and as such it was held that when the executive Government acts as a delegate of a legislative body it had no plenary power to provide for retrospective operation unless and until that power is expressly conferred by the parent enactment and this case was decided following the case report in AIR 1956 (Hyderabad) 35 as referred to above. The next case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of India Sugars and Refineries Ltd. Vs. State of Mysore and others reported in AIR 1960 (Mysore) 326 wherein it was held that the power conferred on the Government under the Madras Sugar Factory Control Act, 1949 to levy did not include a power to impose such retrospectively. In that case by certain notification enhanced rate of sales tax was levied. In that case it was held that unless expressly provided, the power to levy can be exercised only prospectively and not retrospectively. 

 38. The next ground urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the impugned notification (Annexure-B) is bad in law because before issuance of the said notification the petitioner was not given any opportunity to explain his position. In other words, the learned Advocate submitted that the impugned notification is bad for not complying with the principle of natural justice. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Shah Abdur Rahman Vs. The Collector and Deputy Commissioner, Bahawal Nagar and ors. reported in 16 DLR (SC)470. That is a case of removal of a Chairman of a Union Committee without giving any notice to him to show cause and as such the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that although there is no specific provision in the Basic Democracies Order entitling the member proceeded against for giving an opportunity to show cause, the member was entitled to such opportunity on the principle of natural justice. The learned Advocate then referred to the case of Saiyyid Abul Ala Maudoodi and others Vs. The Govt. of West Pakistan and others reported in PLD 1964(SC) 673 and 17 DLR (SC) 209 wherein their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan referred to the case of Shah Abdur Rahman reported in 16 DLR (SC) 470 as already referred. The learned Advocate has also referred to the case of Steamer Agent Association Vs. Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR (AD) 272. In this case the Steamer agent's licence for carrying on LMD business was withdrawn by the authority without giving any prior notice and it was held that the principle of natural justice requiring prior hearing before withdrawal of the licence was required. This case also followed the decision in the case of Shah Abdur Rahman reported in 16 DLR (SC) 470. The learned Advocate has also referred to the case of M/s Hake Mohammad Ali & Sons Vs. Burmah Eastern Ltd. reported in 38 DLR (AD) 41 in support of his contention. In this case the licence for running a petrol pump was cancelled without giving any prior show cause notice and Their Lordships of the Appellate. Division held that -the principle of natural justice was violated in cancelling the licence without giving any notice. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also referred to the case of Commissioner of Income-Tax, East Pakistan Vs. Fazlur Rahman reported in 16 DLR (SC) 410. In this case the respondent filed four applications under Section 33A of the Income Tax Act against certain assessment order but the Commissioner without giving the respondent a hearing dismissed the application and it was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan following the decision in the case of Chief Commissioner, Karachi and another Vs. Mrs. Dina Sohrab Katrak reported in 11 DLR (SC) 113, that mere absence of a provision as to notice cannot override the principle of natural justice. Reference was also made to the case of University of Dhaka Vs. Zakir Ahmed deported in 16 DLR (SC) 722. In this case Zakir Ahmed was expelled from the University for a period of two years without giving any prior notice and the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that the order of expulsion without serving any prior notice was bad for not complying with the principle of natural justice. The learned Advocate lastly referred to the case of Ridge Vs. Baldwin reported in 1963 (2) All England Reports 66. In this case the Chief Constable Ridge was dismissed from service without serving any prior notice to show cause and the House of Lords by a majority judgment held that the order of dismissal was bad for non-compliance of the principle of natural justice. 

 40. So far as the case reported in 16 DLR (SC) 470 is concerned, that was the case of removal of the Chairman of a Town Committee from his office. The case reported in 31 DLR (AD) 272 relates to withdrawal of licence from carrying on LMD business. The case reported in 38 DLR (AD) 42 is also related to cancellation of licence. It is well settled that if an order affects the vested right in property or status or has penal consequences there must be an opportunity to show cause before passing such order. This general proposition of law is not disputed by the learned Attorney-General but he has contended that the principle of natural justice is not of universal application. So far as the decisions of Pakistan Supreme Court are concerned the latest in point of time as has been referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Saiyyid Abul Ala Malldoodi reported in 17 DLR (SC) 209. In that case the then Governments of West Pakistan and East Pakistan simultaneously issued orders under section 16 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1908 declaring the Jamaat-e-Islami to be an unlawful association. These orders were struck down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan finding the said Section 16 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1908 ultra vires the Constitution being inconsistent with the fundamental right Article 7, freedom of association. But all the five learned judges expressed their opinion on the principle of natural justice. Cornelius, CJ agreed with the comment made in Willoughby's Commentary on the Constitution of United States, 1929 Vol. III page 1681 wherein the learned Author reproduced an observation of a learned judge of the New York Supreme Court to the effect that he was "opposed to the judiciary attempting to set bounds to legislative authority or declaring a statute invalid upon any fanciful theory of higher law or principles of natural right outside the Constitution." Cornelius CJ observed that it was a valid comment. SA Rahman, J referring to the cases of Chief Commissioner of Karachi Vs. Mrs. Dina Sohrab Katrak (11 DLR SC 113), M/s. Farid Sons Limited Vs. the Government of Pakistan (13 DLR SC 233) and the Province of East Pakistan Vs. Nur Ahmed (16 DLR SC 375) held that the principle of natural justice requiring a hearing to be granted to a person before being condemned, applies not only to judicial or quasi-judicial proceedings but also to administrative proceeding, provided that the relevant statute does not exclude its application and requires the administrative authority concerned to base its decision on an objective determination of facts. Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, laid much stress on the observation of his Lordship. In the same judgment Fazle Akbar J after referring to' the case of M/s. Farid Sons Ltd. held that the Court cannot question the subjective satisfaction of the Government and thereby held that the question of natural justice was not applicable in that case. Kaikaus, J made general observations without referring to any particular case about the applicability of principles of natural justice in an administrative or a judicial or quasi-judicial capacity but observed that there must be some exception to the general rule. Homoodur Rahman, J after making reference to the cases of Mrs. Dina Sohrab Katrak, M/s. Farid Sons Ltd. and the case of Ridge Vs. Baldwin reported in 1963(2) All England Report 66 observed as follows: 

 In the present case the petitioner also failed to establish that the impugned notification was issued in a discriminatory manners so far as he is concerned because ex facie Article 3 is not discriminatory. In the case of East West Steamship Vs. Pakistan reported in PLD 1958 (SC) 41 Munir, CJ made similar observations as quoted above. In the case of Waris Miah Vs. The State reported in PLD 1957 (SC) 157 Munir, CJ declared section 23 of Foreign Exchange Regulation Act 1947 as unconstitutional being violative of the equality clause because the impugned provision gave power to the Government or the State. Bank of Pakistan to determine whether a person who offends any provision of the Act was to be tried under the ordinary law or by the Adjudication Officer or by a Tribunal. Since the Act as framed made provision for discrimination between the persons falling in the same class the relevant provision of law was declared unconstitutional. In the case of Province of East Pakistan Vs. Sirajul Huq Patwari reported in 19 DLR (SC) 281 a Full Bench of the Dhaka High Court by a majority decision declared section 57 of the Electoral College Act 1964 as invalid and as result thereof the Union Council, Town Committee and Union Committee constituted in the then Province of East Pakistan have been rendered illegal bodies. In reversing the decision of the Dhaka High Court, Hamoodur Rahman, J as his Lordship then was, made the following observations: 

 47. I, therefore, hold that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 is not ultra vires of the Constitution. The last point to be considered is, whether the petitioner is guilty of laches in moving this Court in the Writ Jurisdiction. The learned Attorney-General has submitted that the remedy by way of Writ being extraordinary one the aggrieved person must come to the Court expeditiously and unreasonable delay would disentitle him to such an extraordinary remedy. In support of his contention the learned Attorney-General referred to the case of Standard Vacuum Oil Co. Vs. the Trustees of the Port of Chittagong reported in 13 DLR 804 wherein Murshed, J presiding over the Division Bench observed as follows: 

 He has also referred to the case of Akhtaruddin Khan Vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in 15 DLR 1 wherein Murshed, J presiding over the Division Bench observed as follows: 

 48. Mr. AR Yusuf has referred to the case of Shafiqur Rahman Vs. Certificate Officer, Dhaka reported in 29 DLR (SC) 233 and referred to the observations that in the particular case the petitioner may not rush to the Court on the initiation of the proceeding but when he was threatened with some actual danger he can approach the Court for appropriate relief. In this case the petitioner took lease of the premises of a cinema hall for 15 years for the purpose of exhibiting films. Under the Amusement Act 1923 he used to affix stamps with the cinema tickets issued to the customers and, according to him no amusement tax was due from him; but in spite of that several certificate proceedings for recovery of amusement tax were started against him. In pursuance of the certificate proceedings, distress warrant was issued and some properties were attached. But since the sale proceeds were insufficient, body warrant was issued against the petitioner and at this stage the petitioner filed a Writ Petition in the High Court and it was held that the petitioner was guilty of laches. So this decision is of no help to the petitioner, rather it goes against the petitioner. While disposing of that case their Lordships of the Appellate Division made the following observation: 

 In the instant case before us although the petitioner asserted in his petition that he was a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and it was admitted by all the three Governments namely, the Government of late Ziaur Rahman, the government of Mr. Hossain Mohammad Ershad as well as the present Government that was the reason for which the petitioner did not come to this Court for challenging the impugned notification; but the petitioner's case has similarity with the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 232 inasmuch as the petitioner was aware of the impugned notification as far back in the month of April, and after the change of the Government the petitioner applied for restoration of his citizenship from London but his prayer was rejected as far back in April, 1977 (Annexure-E). Thereafter, the petitioner entered into Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport for a short visit after obtaining visa for three months. After coming over here the petitioner registered him as foreigner and he extended his visa two times and in the meantime he applied for citizenship and the matter is still pending. It is only when that the petitioner was taken into detention under the Foreigners Act that he came to this Court. The petitioner's case is similar to the case reported in 29 DLR (SC) 232 mentioned above inasmuch as in that case the petitioner rushed to the High Court when body-warrant was issued. Although the petitioner tried to explain the delay saying that he was under the impression that he was a citizen of Bangladesh but that cannot be regarded as an excuse for delay in moving the Court in Writ Jurisdiction because the petitioner knows very well that he was no longer a citizen. of Bangladesh, at least since the publication of the impugned notification Annexure- B which he came to learn in April, 1973 and his prayer for restoration of citizenship having been rejected by the Government as far back as in 1977. I, therefore, hold that the petitioner is guilty of laches in coming to the Court in moving the writ petition. 

 59. The most vital question is whether the petitioner because of his absence from Bangladesh from 22.11.71 till his return on 11.7.78, ceased to continue to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh and thereby rendered himself disqualified to be citizen of Bangladesh. On this point Mr. Yusuf has referred the cases of Bishal Deo Tewati Vs. The State, reported in 27 DLR 622. The Advocate General, Government of East Pakistan, Dacca Vs. Benoy Bhusan Majumder and others reported in 25 DLR (SC) 9; Mukhtar Ahmed Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 34 DLR page 29, Mirza Slrahab Ispahani Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in 40 DLR 87 and appeal arising out of it reported in 40 DLR (AD) 117, Hamidul Hoq Chowdhury and others Vs. Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 381; Abdul Huq Vs. Government of Bangladesh and another reported in 33 DLR 113 and the appeal arising out of that decision reported in 1882 BLD (AD) 143. 

 60. The facts of the case of Bishal Deo Tewari, 27 DLR 622, are completely different from the facts of the present case and, as such, I may safely refrain from discussing that case. The case of Mokhtar Ahmed, 34 DLR 29, also is quite distinguishable. In that case the petitioner Mokhtar Ahmed migrated from India to the then East Pakistan and obtained domicile certificate in 1952 and had been living here even after the war of liberation of 1971. He also by an affidavit, expressed his allegiance to Bangladesh on 29.4.72, but due to the situation prevailing in the country at that time he filed an application to the International Committee of Red Cross for going to Pakistan but did not pursue the same and as a result it was rejected. His name was entered in the voters list prepared after the war of liberation and he cast his vote in the referendum held in 1977. Under an impression that a formal citizenship certificate would help him rehabilitate in the society, he applied for the same on 17.3.75. It was rejected by order dated 5.10.77 which he challenged in a writ petition and in that circumstances it was held by a Division Bench of this Court consisting of Mr. Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed (as he was then) and Mr. Justice Rafiqur Rahman, that: 

 62. In Advocate General; Government of East Pakistan Vs. Benoy Bhusan Majumder and others. 25 DLR (SC) 9, the respondents who were residents of the then East Pakistan having their home within the district of Barisal, in November, 1964 went to India on obtaining migration certificate from the Deputy High Commission of India in Dhaka. It may be mentioned here that there was a communal disturbance of some magnitude in that year. Thereafter in 1967 the respondents were found in their village home in the district of Barisal and were prosecuted under section 14 of the Foreigners Act for entering East Pakistan without valid travel documents being citizens of India. The Magistrate found them guilty and accordingly convicted them, which, on appeal, was upheld by the Sessions Judge. On revision a Single Judge of the then High Court Dhaka set aside the sentence. Against that order the Advocate General of East Pakistan moved the Supreme Court of Pakistan and leave was granted to consider if the respondents having gone to India on the strength of Migration Certificate lost their Pakistani citizenship. Their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan after taking into consideration the provisions of sections 3, 4, 6, 7, 13 and 16 of the Pakistan Citizenship Act, 1951 (which with necessary adaptation has become an existing law of Bangladesh) held: 

 64. Mirza Shahab Ispahani, son of a former Chief Justice of the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan, migrated to the then East Pakistan along with his parents after the partition of the sub-continent in 1947. He stayed with his parents in the then East Pakistan upto 1952 when he was sent to England for higher studies. He went there with Pakistan passport and renewed it from time to time. After becoming a Chartered Accountant he secured employment in England and had been staying there for the purpose of earning. With his own income he procured a plot and house in Gulshan Model Town and also hired a flat in Ispahani Colony, Maghbazar, which is the exclusive property of the Ispahani family. During the war of liberation he was staying in London and on 14.4.72 obtained a British Passport which was subsequently renewed. He visited Bangladesh in October, 1972 on the strength of that British Passport and made arrangements for the looking after of his properties here. After his return to England his Gulshan property was treated as abandoned on the plea that he was a citizen of a country which was at war against Bangladesh in 1971 i.e. Pakistan. His repeated representations were turned down by the government whereupon he moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 120 of 1985 and a Division Bench, of which one of us was a member Judge, (40 DLR 87) held- 

 65. Against the decision of the High Court Division, the Government of Bangladesh preferred an appeal and their Lordships of the Appellate Division in that case 40 DLR(AD)117 held: 

 67. In the case of Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury and others Vs. Bangladesh, 33 DLR 381, the properties of Mr. Chowdhury i.e. two daily newspapers and a weekly magazine as well as the press, in which he and his wife held lion's share, were enlisted as abandoned properties and taken over by the government on the ground that the same vested in the government because of the fact that their owners were citizens of Pakistan. Challenging that order of taking over Mr. Chowdhury moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition' Nos. 482 and 483 of 1980. Since the properties in question were taken over as abandoned property treating their owners Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury and his wife as citizens of Pakistan, the question whether they were citizens of Pakistan or of Bangladesh inevitably came up for consideration of the Court. A Division Bench consisting of Mr. Justice Abdul Wadud Chowdhury and Mr. Justice Sultan Hossain Khan, held: 

 69. The last case on which the learned Advocate for the petitioner has relied upon is that of Abdul Huq. Vs. The Government of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 113 and the appeal arising out of it reported in 1982 BW (AD) 143. That petitioner, Abdul. Huq, who happened to be a dealer of ration commodities in Dhaka and trader of betel leaf (pan), was born in Satkhira in 1972 and subsequently lived in Calcutta. However, since partition in 1947 he and his parents were living in erstwhile East Pakistan and continued to live there upto November, 1971 when he went to the then West Pakistan and did not come back from there till the political change took place in August, 1975. Sometime after his return to Bangladesh with Pakistani passport he surrendered the same and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh. His prayer being rejected, he moved the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in its Extraordinary Original Jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution.  72. Prom the decisions and rulings of the High Court Division and the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as well as of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, discussed above, we find that in the case of Mirza Shahab Ispahani the principle laid down which has general applicability is that passport and citizenship are not synonymous. In view of this settled principle of law the fact that petitioner Golam Azam was holding a Pakistani Passport at the time of his arrival in Bangladesh cannot be ground for holding that he has acquired citizenship of Pakistan. In the case of Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, 33 DLR 381, the principle enunciated that prior to the notification dated 18.4.73 Mr. Chowdhury by statutory provision was a citizen of Bangladesh is equally applicable in the case of the present petitioner Golam Azam, because he like Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and like Mr. Chowdhury he was permanently residing in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971 and thereafter, until 'he went to Pakistan in November, 1971. The law enunciated by the highest Court of the country in the case of Abdul Haque 1982 BLD (AD) 143, is more applicable in the present case because the facts of the two cases are almost same and in that case their Lordships of the Appellate Division has held that in spite of his temporary absence the petitioner shall be deemed to continue to be the resident of Bangladesh. Prof. Golam Azam, the present petitioner, in his writ petition has stated that on 3rd December, 1971 he started from Karachi but due to the declaration of war his plane could not land at Dhaka and went back to Colombo and then Jeddah where he had to stay for some days and thereafter all the passengers were taken back to Karachi, that he stayed in Pakistan till December, 1972 as because the government of Pakistan was not allowing Bangladeshis to leave the country and so he took a Pakistani passport for performing Hajj and after performing Hajj he instead of returning to Pakistan, went to London so as to find a way to return to his home country but on reaching there he learnt that he had been declared disqualified to be the citizen of Bangladesh in April, 1973 and so it was not possible for him to approach the Bangladesh Mission in London for granting him Bangladeshi passport. These averments cannot be taken lightly because after the impugned Notification Bangladesh High Commission in London could not issue a passport in his favour. It is evident from Annexure-D attached to the writ petition, that on 20.5.76 he sent a petition addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh for restoration of his Bangladesh citizenship and getting no reply he again sent a petition to the Chief Martial Law Administrator on 12.1.77, Annexure-Dl. There is no allegation from the side of the government that Prof. Golam Azam, the petitioner, applied for or has been granted citizenship of Pakistan. The only allegation against him is that he obtained a Pakistani passport. The prayers of the petitioner were turned down by Annexures-P and P(1), once directly by the Ministry of Home Affairs and again through the High Commission of Bangladesh in UK. Thereafter on his prayer he was granted visa by Bangladesh High Commission in London on receiving clearance from the government of Bangladesh. On the strength of the Pakistani passport and visa granted by the Bangladesh High Commission he reached Dhaka on 11.7.78. He made a fresh application for granting him citizenship on 8.11.78. It may be mentioned here that the learned Attorney-General has laid much stress on the fact that the petitioner on arriving Bangladesh got himself registered as a foreigner and argued that this clearly indicated that he did not treat himself as a citizen of Bangladesh. It may be pointed out that anybody entering into a country with a passport not issued by that country is required to be registered as a foreigner and this is a matter of course only. This in no way could be termed as renunciation of Bangladesh Citizenship. It is not disputed that the petition filed on 8.11.78 for restoration of citizenship of the petitioner has not yet been finally disposed of by the government, or at least, he has not been informed anything in this regard. On the other hand, there are documents attached to the writ petition showing that none else but the Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs in reply to the questions of members, stated in the House of the Nation, that is, the Parliament that the petition of Prof. Golam Azam was under consideration of the government. The last statement in this regard was made on 12.1.92 while the previous statement was made as early as in 1980. From all these facts and circumstance it becomes crystal clear that Prof. Golam Azam never renounced his citizenship of Bangladesh which he acquired by birth and by operation of law. A person cannot be deprived of the citizenship of his country of birth unless be himself renounces it by taking up citizenship of another country in contravention of the law of his country of origin.

 134. Natural justice is nothing but a procedural justice. Being procedural it cannot however be said that it is not vested. This procedural matter speaks of some substantive right, as part of the procedure to be followed in every case where the executive authority decides a matter to the detriment and prejudice of any person. In none of those situations where the natural justice clause is invoked there existed any legal right for such an asking but the matter involves what the court often calls a legitimate expectation of procedural justice'. When that is not specifically ousted by the law itself, the court would read in to the law such a clause. The justice of the common law in such a case will supply the omission of the legislature.
